strings.UKR_GPO_law_desc_0: Generalplan Ost exists to prepare for an eventual German domination of all of Eastern Europe through ethnic cleansing. The Third Phase, beginning in the mid-fifties, has focused less on utilizing mass murder to create this demographic shift, instead using contraception and poor health through limited care to induce a decline in Eastern Europeans. It also has granted increased latitude to local £UKR_bureaucracy_texticon Reichskommissars, who have taken the policy in varying directions - unsurprisingly, Koch has been hardline on the topic.
strings.UKR_GPO_law_1: Finished Third Phase of Generalplan Ost
strings.UKR_GPO_law_desc_1: Generalplan Ost exists to prepare for an eventual German domination of all of Eastern Europe through ethnic cleansing. The Third Phase, which began in the mid-fifties, continued the process through settlement and limitations on Ukrainian livelihoods. With its completion, the £UKR_bureaucracy_texticon Reichskommissariat has met its goals for Germanization over the last five years, capping off fifteen years of fruitful service from the Reichskommissar.
strings.UKR_UNC_law_desc_0: Led by Andriy Melnyk, the Ukrainian National Committee is the sole representative body of the  £UKR_collab_texticon Collaborators, founded by Georg Leibbrandt in order to finance and operate the anti-partisan Ukrainian National Army. Since that time, the UNC has fallen into irrelevance, with Reichskommissar Koch refusing to allow it any degree of importance. Even with his role as deputy, Leibbrandt has been unable to change the situation for his army.
strings.UKR_UNC_law_desc_1: Led by Andriy Melnyk, the Ukrainian National Committee is the sole representative body of the  £UKR_collab_texticon Collaborators, founded by Georg Leibbrandt in order to finance and operate the anti-partisan Ukrainian National Army. Reichskommissar Koch has allowed the UNC a role in government, though only with the strictest of supervision, its powers so limited as to be essentially ceremonial.
strings.UKR_UNC_law_desc_2: Led by Andriy Melnyk, the Ukrainian National Committee is the sole representative body of the  £UKR_collab_texticon Collaborators, founded by Georg Leibbrandt in order to finance and operate the anti-partisan Ukrainian National Army. With an ascendant Leibbrandt, the UNC is now allowed limited advisory and even discretionary action, though intense Reichskommissariat scrutiny and pressure makes it continue to serve as a German mouthpiece.
strings.UKR_UNC_law_desc_3: The Ukrainian National Committee is the sole representative body of the  £UKR_collab_texticon Collaborators, founded by Georg Leibbrandt in order to finance and operate the anti-partisan Ukrainian National Army. However, following the death of Andriy Melnyk, the organization now is unable to proceed with even basic duties, and Security Council gridlock makes replacing the leader near-impossible.
strings.UKR_Bandenbekampfung_law_desc: Under Bandenbekämpfung, The £UKR_military_texticon German garrison is currently empowered to take extreme action against so-called “Bandits”, essentially meaning any partisan forces. This included not only free reign to kill any suspects without process but also freedom to pillage and destroy villages in partisan controlled territory as needed. At present, there are functionally no limits to Garrison action in the field, so long as it is done under these pretenses.
strings.UKR_National_Symbols_Forbidden_law_desc: The Reichskommissariat Ukraine, despite the name, is not a Ukrainian institution. As such, statements of Ukrainian nationalism are forbidden, and this suppression extends even into the visual; symbols of Ukraine are forbidden in public. Even £UKR_collab_texticon collaborators are limited to the designated symbols for the UNA and UNC. Most towns have been redecorated to be “German”, removing symbols of Ukraine and adding £UKR_bureaucracy_texticon Nazi iconography.
strings.UKR_Land_Management_Company_Ukraine_law_: Though much land has been sold off to important and connected German £UKR_industrial_texticon industrialists, a great wealth of Ukrainian territory is still held by the £UKR_bureaucracy_texticon Eastern Ministry (Ostministerium). With their proxy in the Land Management Company Ukraine, the Reichskommissariat holds much of the former Soviet State farms and agricultural machinery, repurposing them to aid the German economy. This gives the RK great latitude with which to shape economic policy.
strings.UKR_SC_law_desc_0: Formed as a temporary measure following the incapacitation of Erich Koch, the Security Council serves as a collective body which functionally operates the government. Composed of leading members of the £UKR_bureaucracy_texticon bureaucracy from all ministries and factions, the Council operates through consensus of its membership, functionally checking the power of the Deputy Reichskommissar - though Georg Leibbrandt is himself a member.
strings.UKR_SC_law_desc_1: Formed as a temporary measure following the incapacitation of Erich Koch, the Security Council serves as a collective body which functionally operates the government. Almost immediately and despite assurances to the opposite, the Security Council has fallen to infighting, as racialists, reformists, and radicals fight over appropriate government policy.
strings.UKR_SC_law_desc_2: Formed as a temporary measure following the incapacitation of Erich Koch, the Security Council serves as a collective body which functionally operates the government. Following negotiations, the body has begun coordinating policy, operating through backroom deals rather than active debates in order to appear unified.
strings.UKR_SC_law_desc_3: Formed as a temporary measure following the incapacitation of Erich Koch, the Security Council serves as a collective body which functionally operates the government. As conditions grow worse, existing informal divides have turned into outright factions, loosely organized but clearly delineated. As the security council was never designed for such a government, effective policy has been made more difficult, though political mobilization has never been easier.
strings.UKR_Dnieper_Mech_law_desc: The region of Southern Ukraine near the Dnieper has seen a renewed modernization drive, bringing its agricultural machinery into the decade. This new investment, made to satisfy the rising grain demands from Germania, should allow for higher yields in the region in coming harvests.
strings.UKR_Decollectivization_law_desc: Following an edict by Erich Koch, planned decollectivization has been completed, taking the remaining state farms and reorganizing them as locally-ran cooperatives. While this limits the government's ability to manage Ukraine's output, this change does make for a more stable and prosperous economy in the future.
strings.UKR_Hungerpolitik_law_desc: The Hunger Plan, originally used during the Second World War to strengthen the £UKR_military_texticon German army, weaken resistance, and allow for future Germanization, has been re-enacted for much of the same reasons. This plan sees Ukrainians given intentionally small rations - most Ukrainians will receive at most half of their daily calories, with those unimportant to the continuing war being given even less, and those in prison barely anything at all.
strings.UKR_nuke.1.desc:
Yuriy and Natasha lived together in a large apartment complex in Kyiv—a complex that they jokingly called the ugliest building in the entire city. Hastily erected during the old Soviet days, with only half-hearted repairs made by the Germans to stop it from collapsing, the ramshackle building seemed like a dirty smudge against the horizon. Yuriy joked that the grime was the only thing keeping the walls glued together.

But these were minor problems. Yuriy and Natasha were living in an age of miracles. Ukraine's hardscrabble militias had pushed further than anyone thought possible. After many weeks of waiting for some great calamity and encountering none, the two had agreed to celebrate.

“The stew smells wonderful, Natasha,” said Yuriy, as he flattened a lace tablecloth against their pockmarked table. The cloth, along with a set of chipped glass goblets, some of the few possessions they'd succeeded in hiding from the Nazis.

There was a laugh. Natasha poked her head from their kitchen. Through the window behind her, he could see a beautiful clear sky marked with a single streak of cloud. “Oh, hush. You only say that because you've only had war rations for the past year.”

“I'm serious!” He insisted. “Any moment, we're going to hear banging on the door from our neighbors, demanding a bowl!”

She rolled her eyes, ready to impress him with more of her glittering wit. It was then, however, that something strange happened. The day behind her seemed to be glowing brighter. Long shadows streaked across the room. There was a terrible rumbling, as if the neighbors truly were breaking down the door, and then a shrill, high-pitched screech that drowned out his wife's last word. “Yur—.”

The window exploded. The goblets shattered. The tablecloth erupted in flames. Yuriy heard screaming and then a feeling of weightlessness as the building collapsed around him.
strings.UKR_nuke.2.desc:
“The flash was so bright. It was brighter than any flash bulb, brighter than the sun. I could feel the air around me growing hot and my body lifting into the air. And then it all went blank. When I woke up, my flesh felt like it was burning from the inside.”

“I saw a young boy—maybe six or seven—stumbling through the street. His skin dangled off his body in little strips. He kept repeating the phrase, 'Water. Water. Water.' I wish I'd had something to give him, but I didn't. I kept walking.”

“Our apartment complex had been damaged in the explosion and, every few minutes, I could feel it swaying in the wind. When I had gotten down to the ground floor, I saw an old man by the name of Mikhail digging through the rubble. I tried to get him to leave with me, but he kept saying that his wife was buried in the rubble and he wouldn't leave without her. He wouldn't go.”

“We ran into the Dnieper. Anything to stop the burning. Anything to get away from the carnage. It was so cold and the water moved so fast that we had to hold onto each other to make sure we wouldn't get swept away. Until I die, I'll never forget how cold the water was, the soft, sticky feeling of our flesh.”

“'Mama! Papa!' The little voices were everywhere. They were coming through the floor from the basement classroom, which had collapsed. Another teacher and I tried for what felt like hours to get them out, but we couldn't get through. Eventually the voices stopped.”

“Those of us nurses who could stand tried to help as much as we could, but it was too much... There was so much pus. Sticky yellow pus. It oozed out of them and soaked the bandages. We knew we had to conserve what supplies we had but they were in so much pain.”

“'Look,' I said after hours of walking. My sister and I looked back for a moment at what had once been Kyiv. All the tall buildings were gone and, on the wind, you could hear the wailing.”
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.1.desc:
And at last, we are free. A strange concept for many, having been laid so low for so long by our former German masters, yet the audacity of the mere notion threatens to intoxicate the mind. From Lutsk to Luhansk, one could hardly fail to hear the ever-present roar of the crowds in celebration of their newfound unity and brotherhood, bearing banners and flying colors that scrape against the skies above. Sons and daughters walk free amongst the golden fields, feeling upon their backs an air that carries the eternal promise of liberation for all who bear it.

And still, something gnaws at the back of our minds. A foreboding presence looms beyond the horizon; a scorned beast that musters still to reclaim their lost prize, circling the band of survivors. Watching, stalking. Licking its teeth. Readying itself for the final strike.

We can no longer deny the inevitable. The Reich is readying its lash, and we may not survive to hear its crack.

What must be done? Faced with losing our newfound independence, we must mobilize our defenses in what shall inevitably become our final struggle for survival. Old stockpiles will be flushed anew with weapons and equipment from our previous struggle. Cities will once again become garrisons, our armies readying themselves against the westward flood. Having enjoyed the brief taste of peace, our stalwart veterans must bid their families farewell one last time and set off to defend their motherland against the Aryan terror. For now, this is all we can do: prepare our materiel and manpower to mount a vast defense across Ukrainian territory in response to the coming storm. Besides that, we have only faith in ourselves and our brothers, sisters, daughters, sons, and the Lord above.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.1.a: Pray for us. Pray for us all.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_tt: £UKR_reichskommissariat Germany is coming, that much is inevitable. We must hold out as long as possible. A decision category has been unlocked for this purpose
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.2.desc:
The beast has finally struck. The combined forces of the Wehrmacht and the Luftwaffe descend upon our lands like a swarm of locusts, drawing a dark void across our skies and throughout the fields of wheat and mud. The hearts of the people are gripped with fear as the thunder of artillery and strafing runs from aircraft draw ever closer to their cities and villages. To the Germans, this is no invasion; this is merely a restoration of order, the correction of an upstart child. They expect nothing less than to neutralize our defenses in one swift blow, hoping that a quick collapse will spell greater fortune for their future maneuvers deeper into Eastern Europe.

Their naked pride is their greatest weakness. They will soon know the extent of our resistance. We have prepared to face the German onslaught on our own terms. Their soldiers think of us as weaklings with no sense of strategy or tactics, yet we take strength in that we have already defeated them once. Our initial victory over their Reichskommissariat demonstrates our strength; we need only show them exactly what the Ukrainian people are capable of.

The weeks to follow will certainly be among the bloodiest in our history. Countless scores of brave men and women will fall to the German menace, and our sons and daughters will soon carry the burden of leading the next generation of freedom fighters in the liberation of their motherland. If we cannot truly defeat them, we will ensure that the lands they inherit will never know peace. Each German settler, soldier, or administrator to come will soon understand the true tenaciousness of the Ukrainian spirit.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_2_tt: The £UKR_reichskommissariat Germans have invaded: our preparation has been converted into bonuses. We must now prepare our insurgency before they conquer us.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.3.desc:
Months of total war have passed since the initial incursions from the Reich into Ukraine. Its toll is becoming ever more apparent upon the expressions of the Hun as their battlelines solidify and their entrenchments grow ever-deeper into Ukrainian soil. Despite their stagnation, they remain persistent in their mission; civil order remains on a knife's edge in the lands they have already occupied, yet the newly-stationed Orpo units refuse to let up any pressure upon our embedded resistance networks.

Attacks from their armies continue ceaselessly, yet the situation on the front has hardly changed. Hardly any new tricks or surprises have materialized from the Reich, and the quiet is near-deafening for our senior military officers. The tension within Kyiv and Germania alike threatens to burst at any moment.

Something is wrong—terribly wrong—and we have no idea what it could be.

Whatever the case, we need to expedite our buildup of an insurgency and prepare our immediate transition as soon as possible. Our approach to open warfare has proven effective to a degree, yet the fact remains that we cannot hope to maintain our current state, especially considering the methods the Germans have yet to employ to ensure their victory. No matter what the Hun may have planned in the coming weeks, we shall endure. This is only the beginning of our long war, and our resolve shall not be broken by even their strongest of weapons and pettiest of trickery.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.3.a: Upon the horizon, the sun is rising.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_3_tt: The £UKR_reichskommissariat Germans are considering extreme actions - the time for insurgency preparations is coming to an end.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.4.desc:
Artem just barely crested the hill before spotting the source of the buzzing hum upon the horizon, spitting out black smoke from one engine whilst it shakily maintained its descending course, struggling to stay within the air. “It's going down!” He turned heel back to his squad at the hill's base, where shouting soldiers quickly boarded their trucks as he raced back downhill. They had been combing the nearby countryside for weeks after several supply networks fell victim to hit-and-run attacks by German settlers. They had struggled for weeks to discern how the settlers were acquiring such weaponry, yet they may have just found their answer, and it was falling from the sky.

Leaping into a truck, Artem gripped his seat as the car sped off along a dirt path, swerving onto the main road as his squadmates checked their gear and rifles. “Told you there'd be some excitement today,” Borys grinned wildly as he playfully gripped Artem's shoulder.

“I doubt there'll be any survivors to—” Artem's retort was interrupted by a distant thud, silencing his squadmates. The airplane must have finally landed, he surmised. Ten minutes passed before they had finally reached the crash site, a Junkers Ju 152 transport now reduced to twisted metal and smoldering wreckage. Its left engine had been reduced to nothing but shattered machinery, while the right's warped propellers continued spinning. Three men, Artem and Borys included, were soon called to comb the intact remains of the transport's fuselage.

Inside was a mess of exposed, sparking wires and scattered metal crates. Borys took point, his rifle at the ready, and approached one of the crates. He took a prybar from his belt and lodged it beneath its lid, tearing the crate open and revealing over a dozen German rifles, numerous pistols, and several grenades. Artem's eyes widened at the mere sight of such weaponry. “Must be for the settlers,” he muttered softly, before Borys took up a Mauser G-3 and briefly inspected it, smiling.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.4.a: “They're ours now,” Borys shrugged, and laughed heartily.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.5.desc:
At first, when the German tanks rolled into Warsaw and Krakow, a strange sense of apprehension filled the streets of Brest. The Wehrmacht's war machine had crushed the hopes of the Polish rebels, but it had stopped there. No one who had survived more than two decades of Nazi rule was foolish enough to believe that would last, but the very fact that the enemy acknowledged the need to prepare for a further advance into Ukraine gave the men and women precious time. Time to build barricades, stock up on whatever supplies could be found, to raise the flag of freedom, to laugh, to love.

But it could never have been enough time. When the first news of a German artillery bombardment on Ukrainian forward positions came in, the dry tinder of frayed nerves ignited into a firestorm of panic. For people who finally had something to lose after so long under the jackboot, the idea of losing it was too hard to bear. Only the intervention of the city's garrison could bring back order to the streets and stop militiamen from fleeing into the forests and desperate townspeople from looting shops.

But a shaky command and shaking hands could only paper over the bubbling terror. The Germans had not come yet, but their arrival was a matter of days. For the grey-faced men and women manning the barricades and the civilians cowering in cellars and gutters, time has run out. They have prepared as well as they could.

And in his makeshift command center, the commander of the city's garrison reviewed his final reports, to see if all their preparation would be enough. As he paced around the table, he knew that there was only one way for him to find out.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.5.a: As night began to fall, his hopes faded with the sun.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_shelling_bad_tt: We have not prepared well enough yet. Time is running out.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.5.b: As the sun set, he saw a ragged detachment waving their flag against the night.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_shelling_good_t: We have prepared well. Time is running out, but Ukraine is not yet lost.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.6.desc:
The smell of soot and blood filled the once-tranquil air as Ivan entered the village square. Olenivka was a tiny settlement, not too far from Kyiv, and was mostly spared fighting in the uprising when the local Auxiliary Police detachment laid down their arms - or at least pretended to. Too many of his detachment had died retaking the village for this to be a simple breakdown of order. This was orchestrated, and Ivan was going to find out by whom.

In front of the small, bullet-ridden church, Ihor and Oleh stood watch over a small group of kneeling men, prisoners who surrendered after their hideout was set on fire. Most were looking at the dirt with empty, resigned eyes. But one young man, no older than twenty, was following Ivan's every step, his eyes blazing with hatred. Catching his gaze, Ivan moved closer and kneeled in front of the handcuffed man. “Who helped you organize this little mutiny, boy?”

The young man spit in Ivan's face. “You fucking bandits are going to kill us all. You went on this damn crusade to liberate a country that never existed on a map, and you never once thought about the actual lives of the people here. Perhaps if you hadn't killed Koch, my brother would still be alive now. This whole uprising of yours was even worse! It's the Germans who decide who lives and who dies in this land, and we never forgot that. We'll see who's laughing when you dangle from the gallows.”

Ivan rose up, wiping the spittle from his face. This was the third such uprising in as many weeks. Former collaborators who feared justice, and feared the Germans even more. Someone on the ground must have prepared these men, ordered them to go underground when the uprising succeeded, and organized these insurrections. They weren't well organized - but that they were organized at all was enough clue that German intelligence was still very much active in Ukraine, working to spread havoc and distrust.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.6.a: “Take them back to Kyiv. We need to know how deep this goes.”
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.7.desc:
When the prosecution witnesses came onto the hastily-repurposed main stage of the Kyiv opera house, the harsh glare of justice seemed inescapable. Oleksandr Ohloblyn, charged with election interference and conspiring with the enemy to bring down the government. Vololdymyr Bahaziy, charged with heading a collaborationist armed formation. The list went on, the silent men accused of almost everything from fraud to murder. The soldiers lining the hall held their rifles in white-knuckled hands, made to stand guard over people they would have rather shot.

When the defendants were given the option to present their case, the light of scrutiny seemed to soften. Most simply begged for mercy, or claimed that they had acted in what seemed to be the best interest of the Ukrainian people at the time. None denied collaborating with the enemy, but many claimed that they've acted to save and help as many as they could in an impossible situation. Behind their imperious desk, the stone-faced judges knew the harsh reality as well as anyone else in the hall - the past two decades were an impossible situation for all who lived them. The People's Republic could at least afford them a fair trial, and look them in the eyes as it did.

When officers of the UNRA came forth to testify on behalf of the defendants, the setting sun's rays seemed to almost caress the hall. The partisan officers underscored that the uprising's success was aided in no small part by sympathetic men within the system. They've also claimed that these men, some of the only Ukrainians who had any experience managing a bureaucratic and economic system of such size, deserved a chance to redeem themselves in the service of Ukraine, which in turn, could not give up talented men in a time of such mortal danger. Could these wayward sons of Ukraine look in their mother's eyes once more?

The final minutes of daylight cloaked the room in red, as the chief justice declared the court's verdict. All eyes were on him.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.7.a: “For treason against the People's Republic, you are sentenced to death by hanging.”
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.7.b: “...due to the prevailing interests of the People's Republic, your prison sentences are to be deferred for the duration of the current emergency.”
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.8.desc:
This was inevitable. That's what the man in a grey uniform told the wailing grandmother, kneeling and hugging the legs of her grandson, still hanging limp in the makeshift gallows erected in the town square. They, the Moskals, the Lyakhs, whoever was deemed an acceptable target had brought this on themselves. He told her they had the privilege of living in his country for centuries and had spitefully never taken up the offer to speak his language, eat his food, or dress like him.

They did not belong here, he told her; her son did not belong here. Yet the old woman in the rags and the butterfly brooch wept all the same. The crowd surrounding the gallows cheered at this spectacle, an elderly man with greying whiskers, a flat cap and a patched-up tweed coat excitedly stamping his foot when the next man on the 'stage' had his chair kicked underneath him and fell for a split-second.

On the main street that ran through the town, the men in grey uniforms spent the last three hours throwing hospital patients of a Russian-owned clinic out of a three story apartment complex sitting on the opposite side of it. The men broke into the intensive care ward of the clinic and had demanded a “liberation tax” from the German menace. Those who could not pay were taken to the apartment complex where they would be dangled off the top balcony and threatened one last time for their valuables. Those who could not pay, fell.

This was inevitable, these men told themselves too. The burning skeletons of shops, the bloated corpse piles in park ponds, the smoke that blotted out the cold, clear day and the humid, wet night - this was all inevitable. Every bullet was deserved, every crime was justice, every atrocity was the result of some centuries-long grievance of the downtrodden rising against the oppressors. Years later, some of these men would succumb to whatever vice supplanted guilt in their psyche. Others took comfort in the violence, cocooning themselves in the warm embrace of nationalism. A small few felt the snag of pity for the children that they had burned, their id unconditionally capitulating to their repressed superego.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.8.a: Yet none regretted what they did.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.9.desc_ukrainiz:
“Despite it all, I'm just glad we still have our liquor!” Ruslan let out a rancorous laugh, much to the chagrin of his two drinking buddies at the dingy wooden table alongside him. Their watering hole of choice—once a hotbed of fierce workers' debates and socialist strategizing, being one of the more underground bars in Siverskodonetsk—had certainly seen better days. Scantly-hanging lightbulbs, flickering in the dusty air as they buzzed with light, just barely illuminated a patchwork of shoddy wooden tables and stools, alongside a bar served by a gentleman of sturdy muscle.

Despite his companion's behavior, Havrylo gave a weak smile before gulping down the last of his glass, letting out a slight groan as the liquid seared his throat. “But,” he wagged a finger, still smiling, “we have kept our pride. Not just as comrades, but as Ukrainians! Never could we have imagined standing so tall in the face of the Germans; even our forefathers would balk at our valor!”

Lidiya sighed at this, rubbing her temples in growing frustration. “You aren't still on about those new laws, aren't you?” The new Ukrainization efforts undertaken by the party delight many Ukrainian nationalists across the republic, including Havrylo. For them, it was a matter of honor, of the spoils of victory following their successful liberation. What were Russians to say of their national trajectory? What might they weakly muse on in the face of an ascendant and authentically Ukrainian revolution?

“Y'know,” Ruslan interjected, his speech beginning to slur with looming drunkenness. “Where'd Dyatlov run off to, anyway? He... he was supposed to meet up here.” Dyatlov, a longtime friend of Levkin, had been a refugee of Moskowien who took up arms for the Ukrainians during the revolution. After today, he would never return to the bar again. In the weeks to come, he would disappear from Ukraine altogether.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.9.desc_toned_do:
“Despite it all, I'm just glad we still have our liquor!” Ruslan let out a rancorous laugh, much to the chagrin of his three drinking buddies at the dingy wooden table alongside him. Their watering hole of choice—once a hotbed of fierce workers' debates and socialist strategizing, being one of the more underground bars in Severodonetsk—had certainly seen better days. Scantly-hanging lightbulbs, flickering in the dusty air as they buzzed with light, just barely illuminated a patchwork of shoddy wooden tables and stools, alongside a bar served by a gentleman of sturdy muscle.

“Well said,” Dyatlov chuckled as he took a swig from his flask, looking to Havrylo beside him. His friend seemed sullen, yet reciprocated the look with a weak smile. “From now on...” He set his flask down, gesturing widely to the group with outstretched arms, “We are all comrades. Russians and Ukrainians, men and women; we are sons and daughters of a brighter future!” The table rang out with cheers and clinking glasses, though Havrylo remained silent still.

Many Ukrainian nationalists had hoped that the government would take a tougher stance on the Ukrainian identity of the revolutionary cause, especially concerning the vocal Russian minorities of the eastern regions of the republic. Havrylo, for the most part, saw the Russians as potential obstacles towards unity; how could a Ukrainian liberation compromise itself by pandering to groups of such little stake in their cause? What if they demanded more still? How far would the party pursue the so-called “unity of the peoples?”

Lidiya touched Havrylo's shoulder, snapping him from his sulking thoughts. She frowned at him, aware of his sullen attitude. “Let it go,” she mouthed, before turning back to the group with a laugh. Havrylo could only sigh as he picked up his glass half-heartedly, giving a laser-fixed gaze to Dyatlov.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.9.a: Havrylo only shrugged. “Didn't feel like drinking, I suppose.”
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.9.b: “Hear, hear.” Havrylo gulped down the last of his glass.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.10.desc:
When news of a ceasefire with the Germans had broken out, Ohloblyn had not expected a parade in his honour or to be sanctified with the greats of Ukrainian history. As he looked outside of his armoured motorcade, heading back to his Presidential Palace, even the men and women who shuffled down the main streets could not help but betray their inner fears. At best, it was passing anxiety. At worst? Ohloblyn imagined they felt what the residents of Paris must have felt when their nation, once a military hegemon, had been humiliated by the Führer. He then mumbled to his chauffeur to drive a little faster.

Peace, however tentative it might be, has come to Ukraine. Throughout the nation, militiamen wait in grim resolve and await the first round of negotiations. After all, their fathers could tell them stories of Germans breaking the peace at the first sign of failure during the Great War. What happens now may not be the peace that the Ukrainian people want but it was the one they would get. Everyone remembered the first time that the Nazis had come to Ukraine. Everyone remembered what had happened to those who resisted the Führer and failed.

The terms of the peace hadn't been decided yet but what media remained in the cities had assured the people that it was a just and fair peace, explicitly not a capitulation. Some almost believed it. Whatever the truth, the easy part was now over. The government now had the breathing room to negotiate survival with, but even returning the country to the living standards it had under Reichskommissar Koch - let alone those of a free, independent nation - would be a gargantuan task. Every single favour will need to be called in, every resource called up and every man put to work. But if we are successful?
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.10.a: Then we will wipe away six hundred years of failure in six.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.11.desc:
A radio crackles from behind a window, its white noise bleeding from two rectangular vents above the storefront. A man's voice escapes, yet is soon smothered by the static. The radio is scarcely heard in the streets of Kyiv; only two men, their heads slumped and faces lined with sorrow, stand to listen to the transmission as others rush by and UPA blackshirts stomp along, truncheons in hand. The static soon fades away into applause, interspersed with jubilant cries of “Slava!” before a voice cuts through the roar of the crowd. “This is a moment of greatness for our people,” resounds Yaroslav Stetsko, the newly-minted Vozhd of all Ukraine. “Hand-in-hand with the patriots of the Reich, our people will ascend to heights never before seen!” The crack of a pistol echoes through the streets, forcing the two men to quickly vacate as the blackshirts run alongside uniformed police.

“...Our sovereignty shall never again be threatened...” A lone officer stands in the doorway of an abandoned barrack, his uniform unkempt and stripped of its insignia. He looks down at a paper clutched in his left hand. “IMMEDIATE DISCHARGE for all standing troops,” it read. His eyes grew wet with tears.

“...Purified economics will lead us to prosperity...” Near Kremenchuk, German agricultural representatives oversee the installation of new mechanized tractors. A joke in German is spoken, and the group laughs; a Ukrainian within the group, the plantation owner, lets out a nervous chuckle. He cannot understand what they intend for him.

“...And we shall cement our place within the unbreakable order of Europe—” A young woman switches off the radio, cradling her child. Sharp breaths escape her lips as she peers out of the nearby window of her cabin, where dark clouds obscure the distant horizon. The darkest of nights would soon consume her nation, and she would never again bear witness to the light of a free Ukraine that once flickered. A fleeting light, yet one she would never forget.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_not_survive_tt: We have abandoned any efforts to oppose £UKR_reichskommissariat Germany.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.100.desc:
Günther was afraid. As he and his companions were driven in Wehrmacht trucks through the city streets, he could not help but notice the eyes of the Ukrainian population, made to greet their returning overlords. It was not fear, or even sorrow, which burned in those eyes. An anger, so simmering it almost made the air around them ripple, radiated from every man, woman and child on the sides of the street. Günther gripped his gun, and swallowed hard. He had the feeling he would have to use it frequently.

Karl was dismayed. A few days occupying his new office in Kiew were enough for a pile of reports to accumulate on his desk, quicker than he could process them. And each one brought worse news than the last. Railway lines being sabotaged. Supply depots raided. Patrols disappearing. Even some open battles, which did not always end in victory for the Wehrmacht. Karl's hands shook as the figures hovered before his eyes. The occupation was as thin as the paper in front of him. The slightest crisis back home would put it in jeopardy.

Ivan was comfortable. He was sitting around a campfire with his friends, drinking and singing. They had all gone underground after the Germans came back, but “underground” did not have to be very deep at all. The German hold on their sector was so weak that he could walk around the nearby village armed without fear. The Germans were the ones having to skulk. Ivan raised his flask and offered a toast to Ukraine and its heroes.

Olha was pleased. The latest shipment of ammunition from the German factory she worked at was prepared, and it would soon be sent to its destination. She trusted that it was in good hands, and the partisans would put it to good use. The Germans were so busy keeping their nose above water that they could not see what was happening right beneath it. Olha smiled. She knew that at some point, sooner or later, they would see. One day, Ukraine will be free.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.100.a: Upon us Ukrainians, fate shall smile once more.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_best_epilogue_t:
Ukraine performed admirably against the £UKR_reichskommissariat German war machine - more than admirably in fact, they have constructed an apparatus of resistance that will sabotage the occupiers for years to come. An organized movement exists for the armed resistance and preservation of the Ukrainian people: clear proof of Ukraine's undying resolve.

There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.101.desc:
Günther was nervous. As he and his companions were driven in Wehrmacht trucks through the city streets, he looked to the Ukrainians lining the streets, made to greet their returning overlords. Their faces were stony, their eyes blank. He could feel their quiet, judging stares piercing him and the other soldiers with a stern judgment. Günther could see those eyes for many nights to come. They were not afraid.

Karl was flustered. A few days occupying his new office in Kiew were enough for a pile of reports to accumulate on his desk, despite his best efforts. The news made for an additional headache. Railway lines were sabotaged, supply depots raided, and in some isolated locations, even small patrols disappeared without a trace. The partisans weren't able to commit to open battles with their material inferiority, at least. Karl put his head between his hands. The occupation was back, but it was not the uncontested ruler of this land anymore. There was much work to do.

Ivan was determined. He was sitting around a campfire with his friends, drinking and quietly singing. They had all managed to go back underground when the Germans came back, and continue to be a threat to the local German garrison. Sympathetic villages in the region were consistently able to provide them with supplies, but Ivan was no fool. He knew that pitched battles and dramatic victories were a thing of the past, and that there was a long struggle ahead. Ivan raised a flask and offered a quiet toast to their success.

Olha was hopeful. The latest shipment of ammunition from the German factory she worked at was prepared, and it would soon be sent to its destination. She hoped that the partisans would be able to take care of it from here. The Germans were busy stamping out the fire they had caused, and many things were able to slip by unnoticed. Olha quietly grinned. She didn't know if the ammunition would reach the partisans, but she had done her part. And that gave her hope.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_good_epilogue_t:
Ukraine performed admirably against the £UKR_reichskommissariat German war machine. Defiance to the occupation is common despite brutal suppression, and organized insurgents bring havoc to the occupiers with a nation rallied behind them.

There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.102.desc:
Günther was quiet. As he and his companions were driven in Wehrmacht trucks through the city streets, he looked to the Ukrainians lining the streets, made to greet their returning overlords. Their eyes were glimmering with the shards of broken hopes, streaks of tears on ashen faces, but there was also something else there - a shred of defiance. Günther shook his head, taking his mind off this pitiful scene to think of happier times.

Karl was busy. A few days occupying his new office in Kiew were enough for a pile of reports to accumulate on his desk, and now most of his waking hours were dedicated to sorting them out. It wasn't bad, all things considered. Most reports were mundane administrative matters, flooding the new administration after the previous chaos. He did get some reports about railway lines being cut and supply lines raided, but Karl didn't worry too much. He'll manage the administration - the Jackboots will do the rest.

Ivan was worried. He was sitting around a campfire with his friends, drinking quietly. They had managed to go underground in those chaotic days when the Germans came back, but it was becoming clear the rest hadn't made it. They did what they could to harass the local garrison, but it was increasingly difficult. Some sympathetic villages cut ties out of fear, and others could not offer them much help. Ivan wondered if the Germans were going to stay here forever. He uncorked his flask and took a long swig.

Olha was dejected. The latest shipment of ammunition from the German factory she worked at was prepared, and it would soon be sent to its destination. The partisan detachment she had tried to send the ammunition to hadn't contacted her in weeks, and she had a sinking feeling that it was too late. All she could do was to cover her own tracks, and hope that the Wehrmacht soldiers who used that ammunition wouldn't harm her or loved ones. It was small, but it was a hope nonetheless.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.102.a: Soul and body shall we lay down for our liberty...
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_bad_epilogue_tt:
Ukraine dared to stand against the £UKR_reichskommissariat German war machine but could not endure for long. The flame of resistance is flickering amongst the storm but it is only a matter of time before the £UKR_reichskommissariat Reich snuffs it out for good.

There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.103.desc:
Günther was proud. As he and his companions were driven in Wehrmacht trucks through the city streets, he looked to the Ukrainians lining the streets, made to greet their returning overlords. Their eyes were broken mirrors, having run out of tears and now only open as windows to an empty husk. Defiance has failed. The only thing these people could still feel was fear. Günther fidgeted with his rifle, ready to turn this land into the Reich's own once more.

Karl was content. A few days occupying his new office in Kiew were enough for a pile of reports to accumulate on his desk, but all things considered, it was simple work. Almost all of it was mundane administrative matters - grain supply, reconstruction, all things that needed to be done after the chaos of the last months. He noted a report about the elimination of a partisan squad near Rowno, and yawned. Karl was an accomplished servant of the Reich. He could afford himself a little break.

Ivan was terrified. He was sitting alone in a dark clearing, an empty flask in his hand. He had managed to go underground in those dark days after the Germans returned, but it quickly became clear that he was likely the only one. He lived off the land, scavenging fruit and hunting small game, staying clear of settlements. The struggle was not against the Germans anymore - it was merely the struggle to survive another day before they found and hanged him. He looked at his flask and once more regretted that it was empty.

Olha was exhausted. The latest shipment of ammunition from the German factory she worked at was prepared, and it would soon be sent to its destination. The Wehrmacht was going to make use of it, pressing the jackboot ever tighter on the Ukrainian people, but Olha did not care anymore. They had risen up, roared their defiance, but it did not matter. The Germans were back, for good. She could only return to work in their factories and pick up the crumbs she was paid. At least she would survive, for now.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive.103.a: A glory and a will, perished.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_worst_epilogue_:
Ukraine, despite the heroic efforts of its people, has fallen to the £UKR_reichskommissariat German war machine. The spirit of resistance that once shined brightly has been put out, leaving only tears and blood. Perhaps one day it will dispel the dark once again; for now, Ukrainian resistance has been crushed by the £UKR_reichskommissariat Nazi jackboot.

There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
strings.UKR_ukraine_romania_interaction.1.desc:
9th ARMY RECONNAISSANCE REPORT: ROMANIAN MOBILIZATION OF TRANSNISTRIAN FRONTIER

FROM: Leonid Henadijovych Ivanov, Kurinny of the 9th Army Reconnaissance Corps

TO: {leader_name}

It is with great disappointment to report that scouts of the 9th Army have confirmed movements of Romanian soldiers along the border between Ukraine and the disputed region of Transnistria, alongside support equipment and resources determined to be intended for a full-scale offensive into the bordering cities of Mykolaiv and Vinnytsia. As such, the need for a coordinated partisan offensive behind Romanian troop movements has become an imperative if we are to resist the coming offensive from both the west and the south. I have already prepared a list of several resistance cells that can be armed and for sabotage operations within the coming weeks, including organizations with access to heavy machinery and motorized vehicles, which you can find on page six of this document.

Successful partisan operations could significantly harm the Romanian war machine and disrupt further mobilization along the Transnistrian region, reducing our potential southward burden of soldiers and allowing us to focus our full attention upon the Reich and the bulk of the Wehrmacht's forces westward. Brave patriots of the Ukrainian cause are spread far and wide outside even our own borders, ready to take up arms once more and fight for the continued independence of their homeland. As a military officer, I believe these patriots will prove indispensable in the confrontation that shall soon arise between our motherland and the lackeys of the Aryan beast.
strings.UKR_ukraine_romania_interaction.1.a: The true war is fought on the back line.
strings.UKR_ukraine_romania_interaction.2.desc:
9th ARMY RECONAISSANCE REPORT: UPRISING IN MOHYLIV-PODILSKYI

FROM: Leonid Henadijovych Ivanov, Kurinny of the 9th Army Reconnaissance Corps

TO: {leader_name}

With great pleasure, I write that our efforts in arming Ukrainian resistance groups across the Transnistrian region have successfully borne fruit, as demonstrated in the recent clash between partisan organizations and the Romanian 1st Security Division at the border of Mohyliv-Podilskyi. Tensions have remained steadily rising within the city for much of the past decade due to the inaction of the Romanian government regarding local representation. Yet, it was our guns and equipment that successfully lit the spark of liberation aflame and beset the Romanian dogs with the might of countless Ukrainian patriots.

The border between our state and the Transnistrian administration has already begun to falter, with hourly reports of new skirmishes between partisans and stationed Romanian army garrisons alongside the Dniester. Additionally, our embedded agents within Transnistrian organizations have reported that a growing number of partisans have begun leaving many of the “old guard” resistance organizations in favor of groups directly supporting the Kyiv government. This may prove to be quite the boon in future operations between our soldiers and partisan groups, as well as easing any ideological tensions that may arise in fighting side-by-side. A complete list of these friendly partisan organizations can be found on page seven of this report, alongside their most notable leaders and geographical operations.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_category_desc: While we have liberated our country from the £UKR_reichskommissariat German yoke, this will not last for long. £UKR_reichskommissariat Germany refuses to give up its breadbasket and will soon come for us. While we stand no chance against them, we must prepare as much as we can and build up resistance, so that their occupation will be miserable. Failure to prepare is not an option. If we hold out without finishing our insurgency, £UKR_reichskommissariat Germany may take desperate measures.
strings.UKR_Ukraine_Must_Survive_Status_preparat: We are as prepared as possible
strings.UKR_Ukraine_Must_Survive_idea_desc:
Stability: [?UKR_ukraine_must_survive_rewards|%+=]
War Support: [?UKR_ukraine_must_survive_rewards|%+=]
Division Attack: [?UKR_ukraine_must_survive_rewards|%+=]
Division Defense: [?UKR_ukraine_must_survive_rewards|%+=]
Division Organization: [?UKR_ukraine_must_survive_rewards|%+=]
Division Recovery Rate: [?UKR_ukraine_must_survive_rewards|%+=]
--------------
The spring of independence has ended, and now comes the bitter harvest. The great scythe of the German reaper, drenched in the blood of millions, rises again upon the fertile fields of its so-called “breadbasket”, as inevitable as winter follows fall. Millions of souls stand before it, shivering in the wind, waiting for its shadow to fall upon them once more.

But they will neither go quickly nor quietly. The independent Ukrainian government has gathered its resources and built up its forces to fight against the invading Wehrmacht. No one believes that Ukraine will be able to halt the enemy advance on the battlefield, and Ukraine's resources are depleting too quickly to match a continent's worth of industrial might. But the defenders of this black earth are determined to water it with German blood for every inch they gain.

Germany is engaging in a massive terror bombing of cities and towns across Ukraine to destroy industry and infrastructure to collapse the Ukrainian war effort. Already, military production has fallen massively and logistics have gotten much harder. Hint that things are only going to get worse as this goes on.
strings.UKR_terror_bombing_desc:
With the situation in Germania once again stabilized, the Luftwaffe has been unleashed upon Ukraine in an effort to decimate production and pulverize our people into submission. German planes buzz overhead day and night, dropping hundreds of tons of death and destruction upon Ukraine's fields, towns and cities.

Our soldiers are tenacious, but as their fortifications are obliterated, they know they cannot stem the tide. Our workers are motivated, but as their factories are reduced to rubble, they know they cannot match Europe's industrial juggernaut. Our government is committed, but as villages are wiped off the map, they know that their time is running out. And they all know that the German jackboot does not tolerate defiance. The longer we last, the worse the punishment will be.
strings.UKR_terror_bombing_2_desc: Already rubble, the cities have been pulverized further by a Luftwaffe that strafes anything larger than a housecat. With even the outhouses bombed, producing anything of worth to the war is now impossible. If we do not do something, we will be buried under the rubble too.
strings.UKR_broken_breadbasket_desc:
Across Ukraine, the black soil runs crimson with blood. Following the German occupation, civil order in Ukraine teeters on the brink of collapse, with the countryside plagued by nigh-permanent partisan activity while urban terrorist cells mount increasingly complex bombings and hit-and-run attacks upon German administrators. Pacification of the former Reichskommissariat, once thought of as a simple errand by the Wehrmacht's top brass, has proven an abysmal failure.

The economy lies in shambles, barely clinging to life through inadequate German aid packages regularly stolen by partisan groups, leaving only scraps left for settlers. Grain production remains a difficult venture at best; an impossibility, at worst. For as long as she might continue to live on, Ukraine will never know peace, and any prospect of stable governance under the Reich now lies bleeding upon the soil.
strings.UKR_unstable_breadbasket_desc:
Across Ukraine, the black soil has grown arid and lifeless. Domestic instability and growing resentment from the native population have plagued German occupation forces since the fall of the partisan regime, complicating the efforts to contain a persistent insurgency that permeates the rural countryside. Ukraine's occupiers face near-daily harassment by resistance cells, and a large-scale campaign of suppression has been met with mixed results and a further galvanized native population.

Relentless sabotage and open warfare have left the economy in ruins. Ukraine's once-proud grain industry struggles for stable footing under the new administration. Any pacification of these afflicted regions is anticipated to be a years-long undertaking, leaving German officials to watch with dread as their grip upon Ukraine grows ever more tenuous.
strings.UKR_enduring_breadbasket_desc:
Across Ukraine, the black soil springs anew with life. German officials had repeated platitudes that the previous partisan regime was an inherently weak institution, yet many remain surprised to witness the relative stability of the German occupation. Resistance forces remain disorganized and isolated, unable to properly organize coherently or gather new equipment, rendering their struggle futile in the face of a reorganized German administration.

Efforts to stabilize the Reichskommissariat's economy remain tenuous, yet progress continues at an encouraging pace. Grain production is expected to meet quota levels in the medium term. Though the situation remains unstable, the complete pacification of Ukraine is expected to be achieved in the years to come with relatively minimal effort.
strings.UKR_restored_breadbasket_desc:
Across Ukraine, the black soil blossoms anew with bountiful harvest. Following a lightning blitz by the Wehrmacht across the Ukrainian countryside, securing key objectives and urban centers with little delay, the German occupation of the errant Reichskommissariat is expected to be a trifling affair by many in the highest echelons of the Reich.

Exhausted by conventional warfare and lacking the resources, manpower, and respite to reorganize, even the strongest partisan groups can no longer mount a meaningful insurgency. Outside of lone wolf attacks targeting logistical operations and local businesses, the renewed occupation remains effectively unopposed by the native population, and German officials remain hard at work at restoring government authority, expediting reconstruction efforts across the countryside, and enforcing new agricultural quotas levied by the Reich.
strings.UKR_ticking_to_oblivion_desc: This is not a war we can win. The Reich's resources are endless; ours are rapidly depleting. We will wither away - what time we have must be dedicated to preparing our long-term insurgency.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_ticking_to_obli: Every week, we will lose the benefits of our preparation and eventually begin taking penalties.
strings.UKR_german_morale_decreases_desc: £UKR_reichskommissariat Germany expected this campaign to be a quick restoration of their rule. They were wrong. We will make them pay for every meter of soil with blood. As we hold strong, their morale will decline, but they will take increasingly desperate measures to win.
strings.UKR_German_Morale_Decreases_0_tt: Illusions of a quick invasion are dashed as a bombing campaign is prepared.
strings.UKR_German_Morale_Decreases_1_tt: Terror bombing campaigns are waged across Ukraine as the Reich debates general mobilization.
strings.UKR_German_Morale_Decreases_2_tt: The Reich has begun general mobilization as panic breaks out in Germania.
strings.UKR_German_Morale_Decreases_3_tt: Panic is gripping the German nation while the offensive stalls.
strings.UKR_German_Morale_Decreases_4_tt: The situation has gotten eeriely quiet.
strings.UKR_restart_military_industry_desc: The war to liberate Ukraine has left it in ruins but what little industry we have left is geared solely for war. We must expand on this base, rebuild destroyed factories, and produce as much equipment as we can.
strings.UKR_train_wartime_conscripts_desc: In the fury of war, we had to engage in mass conscription of men with little to no training. We must reverse this trend. We will begin a program to train these conscripts so that they can be effective soldiers.
strings.UKR_crush_german_remnents_desc: The collapse of the Reichskommissariat wasn't enough. The Germans in their hubris continue to fight us, hoping to restore their colonial rule. We must root them out decisively.
strings.UKR_requisition_food_for_stockpiles_desc: The horrors of war have left millions hungry. In order to minimize famine, we must stockpile and distribute food via government directive. With the Germans at the gates, we have no other option.
strings.UKR_fortify_the_german_border_desc: While the Reich hasn't attacked us yet, they will soon. Trenches must be dug, bunkers built, and defense networks expanded if we want to delay their onslaught.
strings.UKR_fortify_the_romanian_border_desc: The Germans will not be alone in their invasion. To our south lies Romania, another colonial power, fearing that a free Ukraine would liberate Transnistria. We must prepare our border with them.
strings.UKR_fortify_the_ostland_border_desc: The colony of “Ostland” may have faced substantial disruptions, but the Germans are likely to secure it before attacking us. To secure our northern flank, we must make sure that the border is protected.
strings.UKR_encourage_rebellion_in_transnistria_: With the length of our front line with the invaders, we need to exploit all opportunities available. One of these is Transnistria - Ukrainian land. We must enable rebellion in the region to slow down a southern attack.
strings.UKR_german_settler_uprising_desc: Enraged by the abolition of their privileges and the destruction of their colony, the invaders gather together into “Freikorps” militias dead set on taking down our government. While they cannot overthrow us outright, they are quite the hassle.
strings.UKR_german_sabotage_desc: Germania is not silent as its breadbasket breaks free. No, it sends agents into our country, sabotaging industry, assassinating officers, and enticing the weak-willed to rebel against us.
strings.UKR_rival_partisans_rise_up_desc: Alas, the Germans are not our only enemy. Many of our countrymen reject our leadership, clinging to the remnants of failed partisan groups that hope in vain to take the lead from us.
strings.UKR_FUK_collaborators_selling_out_desc: Our forces relied on the cooperation of several ex-collaborators. Now, with Germany preparing an invasion, these collaborators reveal themselves to not be so “ex” at all, revealing our secrets and plotting against us in exchange for empty promises.
strings.UKR_BOV_civilian_massacres_desc: Our army is barely under our control. Rogue units rampage across villages - Communist, German, Polish, Russian, or otherwise - to murder anyone they deem to be traitorous or poisonous to the nation.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_go_underground_: We have survived the first wave.
strings.UKR_go_underground_desc: It is time. We cannot withstand the onslaught much longer. Our preparations for the transition to insurgency have gotten as far as they can. It is time to go underground and cease the conventional war - our government will officially dissolve and escape underground along with as many soldiers as possible.
strings.UKR_go_underground_tt:
We will go underground, locking us into our insurgency preparation and capitulating within a few days.
To get the best possible insurgency, we must have a preparation of at least 90%. The results of our efforts will be revealed in an event a few days following our capitulation.
strings.UKR_ukraine_must_survive_preparation_pha: We are preparing for the German invasion.
strings.UKR_UCW_ongoing: The Ukrainian Civil War is ongoing!

there's three guys three heads get it yeah this is the power struggle dynmod please loc me!!
strings.UKR_galicia_buffs_racist_desc: The UPA has some Galician guys so we get buffs.
strings.UKR_BOV_shukhevych_dominant_desc: Roman Shukhevych, long-time commander and critic within the OUN-B, has used his allies to have a near-total influence on UPA field policy. Shukhevych's mass influence means the UPA will be disciplined and yet muted, pragmatically weighing its next moves.
strings.UKR_BOV_stetsko_dominant_desc: Yaroslav Stetsko, the unusual Germanophile activist with the UPA, has managed to worm his way into power. With Stetsko at the lead, the OUN-B will likely be more disciplined than ever, but Stetsko's lack of natural charisma or message will limit the effectiveness of his army.
strings.UKR_BOV_klyachkivsky_dominant_desc: Dmytro Klyachkivsky, the most radical of the OUN-B's leading members, is unquestioned in his role as the Vozhd. As such, he will push the UPA even further than ever, but this will come at a cost.
strings.UKR_BOV_unified_OUN_desc:
The OUN is supposed to be an outlet for Ukraine's very spirit, just as Bandera imagined it - it is supposed to speak in one voice, an outlet for a nation screaming out while so many wield all they can to suppress it. Yet even in victory, too many felt able to debase their nation through disloyalty. Under Shukhevych, these people will stay by our side, but they will be reminded that their duty is not to their vanity, but to a higher power.

They will not speak, not because they are broken, but because they see the light.
strings.UKR_BOV_Purged_OUN_desc:
In the past, the OUN was filled with rot. Those who did not listen, those who did not follow, those who did not trust. A great mass of men and women who refused the call of the Vozhd.

Their end has come.
strings.UKR_BOV_the_polish_scourge_tt: The Poles, long occupiers of our rightful land, will soon face justice.
strings.UKR_BOV_exterminate_melnyks_vermin_tt: There shall be no mercy for Melnykite splitters.
strings.UKR_BOV_operation_golovinsky_tt: It is time to set wrongs right.
strings.UKR_BOV_last_roman_tt: At last, reason has returned to Ukraine's patriots. Klyachkivsky's madness and Stetsko's treason have been crushed - liberty awaits us!
strings.UKR_BOV_shattered_front_tt: First, let us mend old wounds.
strings.UKR_BOV_uneasy_truce_tt: Peace at last, for now at least.
strings.UKR_BOV_ukrainian_triumvirate_tt: One man - one Vozhd - cannot rule alone.
strings.UKR_BOV_excise_extremist_excess_tt: Some of us have not gotten the memo it seems. Unfortunate. They will have to go.
strings.UKR_BOV_fractured_organization_tt: Let us bring justice, and thus unity, to our people.
strings.UKR_BOV_emboldening_embers_tt: Let us stand together. We will die alone otherwise.
strings.UKR_BOV_a_score_unsettled_tt: The Poles will given a chance to see reason.
strings.UKR_BOV_fortune_infamous_tt: It didn't have to be this way, but it's too late now - Klyachkivsky and Shukhevych are dead.
strings.UKR_BOV_yaroslavs_wisdom_tt: Refusal to collaborate is simply a refusal to grow - an insistence on suicide, if you will.
strings.UKR_BOV_twist_the_dagger_tt: There shall be no more dissent in my Ukraine.
strings.UKR_BOV_reassure_settlers_tt: We are liberators, not butcherers. Our German friends will surely see this.
strings.UKR_BOV_bloodlands_await_tt: We shall reclaim our rightful land from Polish rot.
strings.UKR_BOV_klyachkivsky_epilogue_tt:
The £UKR_UPA Ukrainian Insurgent Army, once a fringe partisan organization doomed to extinction, has received a new lease on life and brought independence to Ukraine after twenty years of subjugation. Klyachkivsky has at last solidified his throne with the blood of his enemies, yet so many more are to follow.
There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
Until then, you can continue taking decisions in the “Against Goliath” decision category - granting you another ending should you choose to continue playing without a focus tree!
strings.UKR_BOV_shukhevych_epilogue_tt:
The £UKR_UPA Ukrainian Insurgent Army, once a fringe partisan organization doomed to extinction, has received a new lease on life and brought independence to Ukraine after twenty years of subjugation. But the crimes of the past cannot be repaid, nor the German threat forever stopped - all that remains is a struggle to remember.
There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
Until then, you can continue taking decisions in the “Against Goliath” decision category - granting you another ending should you choose to continue playing without a focus tree!
strings.UKR_BOV_stetsko_epilogue_tt:
The £UKR_UPA Ukrainian Insurgent Army, once a fringe partisan organization doomed to extinction, has received a new lease on life and brought independence to Ukraine after twenty years of subjugation. With the fall of Klyachkivsky they have changed their tune, but will their German masters accept their call?
There is more to come for Ukraine in the future to complete this story, but from the entire Ukraine team, thank you for playing - we hope you enjoyed it as much as we did making it!
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon_activa: Activate Three Heads of the Dragon
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon_tt: The Heads of the Dragon will begin to fight amongst themselves.
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon_dynmod: The Three Heads of the Dragon
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon: The struggle between the Three Heads of the Dragon is ongoing
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon_gui_kl:
Dmytro Klyachkivsky
------------------
Dmytro Klyachkivsky has been the leader of the £UKR_UPA UPA since its establishment, yet his leadership has finally come into question. Following the tenets of Dontsov, he commands his insurgents with an iron fist.

Purging Ukraine of its weakness is the only way for it to become free and Klyachkivsky has no qualms with doing what must be done, consequences be damned. The Teuton menace can only be repelled by an indomitable spirit with an indomitable will, and he's the man for the task.

Ukraine indivisible is the only Ukraine that will withstand the storm.
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon_gui_st:
Yaroslav Stetsko
------------------
Yaroslav Stetsko is a civilian among the £UKR_UPA UPA, a rarity, yet he's a man with potent influence and immense sway. He has built a clique around him of close allies within the £UKR_UPA UPA's civilian arm and now he seeks to wrestle control away from the military leadership.

Stetsko's promises of peace and prosperity pull prospective followers towards his grasp, but one can easily wonder if he's offering far more than he can actually deliver. Regardless, he has intellect, charisma, and the ambition to see his will done.

Perhaps in this era of great despair, a bold man with a vision is the beacon of light Ukraine needs?
strings.UKR_BOV_three_heads_of_the_dragon_gui_sh:
Roman Shukhevych
------------------
Roman Shukhevych is the £UKR_UPA UPA's second highest ranking officer. Having taken the malcontents of the £UKR_UPA UPA under his wing, Shukhevych has established a power base in opposition to Klyachkivsky's derangement.

Shukhevych is a unity figure before anything else and his own political leanings make him a questionable man to rally behind, yet his disinterest in political affairs has allowed for some dissent to flow freely as a newer generation of ideologists seek to seize the reins.

Yet one can only wonder if a man unashamed of his bloodstained past is truly capable of rebuilding the bridges he's burnt.

strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.1.desc:
“Chairman Melnyk? Chairman Melnyk? I have your morning tea. Melnyk?”

With his left foot, Melnyk's secretary pushed open his superior's office door, expecting to hear a weak greeting from the Chairman. Instead, Melnyk was silent, his torso slumped onto his desk, his skin made pale and sallow by rigor mortis or by office lights. The secretary put down the teaset and checked his pulse. Nothing.

The secretary bowed his head for a moment. Perhaps in better days, his first thought would have been on memorials and decorum, Melnyk would have liked. But there was no time for such niceties. Quietly, as if not to disturb him, the secretary pushed Melnyk's heavy frame aside and reached for his telephone. A few people would need to be called - Melnyk's wife, his few lasting friends, Leibbrandt. First, however, came succession.

~~~

“...yes? Yes? I understand. My condolences to Pan Melnyk. He was a great leader for the Ukrainian people, despite our differences.”

Pavlo Shandruk expected he would have a great reaction to the news. Melnyk was a fellow veteran of the Sich, a freedom fighter for Ukrainian, a long-time acquaintance. But all Shandruk could think of was their meetings together - Melnyk pointing at a map, relaying German instructions, telling the old general which villages needed to burn.

Instead, Shandruk chose to focus on politics. “Before you consult anyone else about this matter, I am going to give you a list of names. Inform them of the news, discreetly, and tell them to message me at their earliest convenience. We are going to have a meeting of the Ukrainian National Council in the following week, and we must stand as a united front to choose a successor. As for the Reichskommissar...”
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.2.desc:
Kozhevnikov's voice was crackled and warped, but his words were clear. The UNC had discovered that Andriy Melnyk had died in the night. Georg Leibbrandt, from his manor in the south, was already arranging papers and giving notes. Kozhevnikov was Leibbrandt's most loyal protégé, one of the few Ukrainians who he knew he could trust implicitly. He clearly needed to be the successor.

Yet doing so meant propelling a fairly controversial man into the top slot. Yes, the Ukrainians were intelligent in their own way, but they also had consistently proven in need of guidance during times of crisis. After all, it was their own radical and warped kind who attempted revolution. Their psychology was one of loyalty, of leadership, and it only took a small number of disgruntled and motivated leaders to pull them in every direction. The moment divisions appeared, the Security Council would have an excuse to step in and create a crisis.

A party line was needed. If Kozhevnikov was to be the next Chairman, he could have no opposition.

Leibbrandt put down the phone and called for his secretary. Still buried in his notes, he barked out an order to the man. “Call Sushko, Shandruk, Shtul, even Stsiborskyi. Any UNC member who might try to take the role. Tell them all that, for reasons of national unity in this time of mourning, they are to stand down and support the candidacy of Herr Kozhevnikov. Don't let them argue, give the order and move on.”
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.2.a: “If I know the Ukrainian people, they'll listen.”
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.2.b: “If I know the Ukrainian people, they'll listen.”
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.2.c: “If I know the Ukrainian people, they'll listen.”
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.3.desc:
The air brought tidings of change, yet Artem felt nothing really different. Of course, his work in the grand scheme of things was minimal at best; on his dutiful page, he wrote the letters and missives to be sent, from the higher-ups, towards the officers and bureaucrats through Ukraine. It was a dull job to be sure, but it afforded him a thoroughly peculiar point of view of the minds that ruled over the Reichskommissariat. His fingers dutifully clack at the letters, checking the missives he read to make sure the message is sent along properly.

Yet, something in him feels the ever-present sense of...boredom? Disappointment? Even with the turmoil of changes, with the growing tensions, a climate he could feel every day he walked back to his office, he still turned to this table, to write the same messages in an almost robotic motion; as if nothing was wrong.

It's in this growing haze of monotony, that perhaps a simple spark lit in his head. And he only really needs to look upward, to the picture hanging in his dull, beige office to remember why the UNC is acting through the motions. It used to show the portrait of Melnyk, but from one day to another, perhaps in the cleaning of the offices, it was swiftly replaced before anyone could even grieve.

For it's not the temperate expression of the deceased Andriy Melnyk that gazes at the offices, but of Leibbrandt, berating him for wasting time looking at the portrait.

Without lifting a single word, without even a public appearance, just with a casual swap of a portrait, it was like the whole party had their leash pulled...and they could do nothing for the moment, lest the turmoil that rages outside consumes them whole.
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.3.a: With a resigned sigh, Artem went back to work.
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.4.desc:
It's perhaps baffling how context can change how one perceives their surroundings, and Shandruk would know that better than most men. After all, a battlefield can have many meanings, and all it takes is a single moment, a single shot, a single bombshell, to radically change a victory to a crushing, costly loss. And in the halls of the Kiew's political elite, the most dangerous game is being played, not initially with guns, but certainly ending with one if they aren't careful.

The lock is checked, double-checked, triple-checked. A red telephone is set on the counter, ready to be ringed if this meeting goes south and an evacuation is necessary. The windows are covered, the lamps dimmer, and Shandruk's personal gun is in his lap. Tapping his fingers, nails overgrown and unkempt, he stares at his fellow UNC-S members, their faces barely betraying the anxiety and nervousness. In the end, recruits didn't change, be them wearing uniforms or suits, the fear of death and reprisal is always a haunting mirage when one seeks to change something.

“...what you're suggesting is outrageous at best, and treasonous at worst. In any ideal circumstance, I would have you shot.”

“Sir, if you...forgive me speaking, but as it stands, we're liable to end up purged by Leibbrandt anyway. Any slight to his 'vision' is something to get rid of, and it's not a matter of if...”

The young man stares at his face, his eyes glancing over at the closed windows for a moment, leaving the old veteran to ponder: what else is that man worried about, besides his own skin.

“...but when? Bräutigam is our best bet, sir. You know that.”

A silence stretches in the office before Shandruk clicks his tongue and goes to the phone, dialing a long repeated number. It's ludicrous, suicidal even, but he's right. Bräutigam has shown strength in this chaotic mess, and people like him and his party would be nothing but stains for Georg to wipe away in his vision of a perfect Ukraine.
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.4.a: Bohdan, get me a meeting with Bräutigam. Be discreet, our necks are on the line for this.
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.5.desc:
“This is a bloody disgrace.”

“What, the office?”

“Yes. Albeit it's not what's in here, but what's missing from here.”

Sushko raises his brow as Stsiborskyi scoffs, reaching into his pocket for a wallet of cigarettes. He thought Stsiborskyi would offer him one, but he simply lit one with a single match before tossing it out the window. Sushko raised one eyebrow, willing Stsiborskyi to speak, which simply lead to an awkward silence as the aides removed more traces that Melnyk ever existed. Soon enough, aides shooed the two out of the office, their steps bordering on automatic until Stisborskyi's firm hand held Sushko's shoulder in place, in the middle of the staircase leading to the second floor.

“Please don't tell me you're going to go ahead with Leibbrandt.”

“Of course not. That man is a bootlicker of the highest caliber. But do you have any suggestions? Because I'm not willing to be in tomorrow's obituary.”

“We just need an ally. Someone who can be our public face. How about Bräutigam?”

“He's a failed candidate at this point - if he'd even work with us.”

“And obviously not Koch, the man's a bloody vegetable.”

It was a small blessing that their surroundings were deathly silent as both men spoke of treason. Yet, as both politicians' mental lists ran down, one particular name remains, to their growing distaste and horror.

Otto Ohlendorf. Someone with enough power, and enough ambition to champion their cause. They'd help launder his reputation, and he could protect them. It made them ill to the core.

And yet no one else fit. They had to tie their destiny, to that farce. Hands shaking and with grim acceptance on both of their faces, they share a quiet nod and climb upstairs, acting as naturally as they could...
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.5.a: ...as both willingly let the Scorpion climb on their backs.
strings.UKR_pwr_struggle.6.desc:
The phone clicked as it was placed back into its receiver, and Ohlendorf felt a pang of regret strike him as the “alternative backchannel” confirmed his worst fears. Readjusting to his new circumstances, Ohlendorf laid back in his chair, and reflected on what could only be his latest course of action.

With the collaborators apparently firmly within Leibbrandt's pockets, he'd been locked out of a potential family of assets. Of course, collaborators rarely made good political allies, and a German with a club was just as strong as a Ukrainian, if more trustworthy. As lamenting what could have been certainly had been no more than a distracted man's waste of time, Ohlendorf began dialing Weinmann.

“It's final, then? We've lost the UNC?” The perspiration over the line was tangible, though Ohlendorf could not find it in himself to partake in the stress.
